branches.theme: Prose Narrative: Animals, Birds, and Dr. Dolittle (Hugh Lofting)

sub_branches.concept: Transition from Human Medicine to Veterinary Care
details: Dr. John Dolittle lives in Puddleby-on-the-Marsh and treats human patients who complain ungratefully.
The Cat's-food-Man suffers from a stomach-ache and suggests Dolittle become an animal doctor.
Argues that local veterinarians lack true understanding of animal ailments.
Dr. Dolittle loves animals and agrees that treating them would be far more fulfilling.
evidence_or_examples: The Cat's-food-Man pointing out that Dr. Dolittle knows more about animals than all local vets combined.

details: Polynesia the parrot reveals that animals possess complex languages comprising vocal phonetics and non-verbal signs.
Translates bird language: 'Ka-ka oi-ee, fee-fee' means 'Is the porridge hot yet?'.
Explains silent animal signetics: nose twitches, ear movements, tail wags, and eyelid flutters.
Dr. Dolittle gets his butcher's notebook and pen to systematically record animal vocabulary.
evidence_or_examples: Polynesia dusting cracker crumbs off her wing while teaching the doctor bird phonetics.
Dogs twitching their nostrils to ask questions without barking.

details: Dr. Dolittle opens a specialized clinic for domestic pets, working animals, and farm livestock.
Diagnoses pugs, poodles, cows, and plough horses by listening directly to their complaints in their own tongues.
Rejects generic veterinary remedies in favor of targeted, sympathetic treatments.
Gains widespread renown as a true animal scholar and master of inter-species communication.
evidence_or_examples: Old ladies bringing pugs sick from eating sweet cake; farmers bringing cows with eye troubles.

details: Classification of Compound Words into three distinct types:
1. Closed Compound Words: joined without spaces (windowsill, flowerpots, teatime).
2. Open Compound Words: written with spaces (bird language, plough horse, harvest mice).
3. Hyphenated Compound Words: joined by hyphens (Cat's-food-Man, check-in, well-bred).
Usage of present perfect tense for recent past actions with present relevance.
evidence_or_examples: Analyzing text examples across all three compound word categories.

branches.theme: Humorous Poem: A Funny Man by Natalie Joan

details: Describes an encounter with an extraordinarily eccentric figure.
The funny man wears two hats on his feet instead of shoes.
Walks and hops home balanced upside down on his head.
Eats a currant bun while staggering in an inverted posture.
evidence_or_examples: Visual contrast of shoes on head and hats covering feet.

details: Combines ridiculous physical appearance with formal, courtly speech.
Addresses the ordinary passerby speaker politely as 'Your Highness'.
Uses alliteration in phrases like 'funny sounding sight' and 'hopped home'.
Creates lighthearted wit through the juxtaposition of absurdity and formal manners.
evidence_or_examples: The funny man tipping his foot-hat while bowing and saying 'Good day, Your Highness'.
